doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Discontinuity of musical language since the late 1960s
summary: Israels says the break in musical tradition after the late 60s, from Gershwin to Lloyd Webber and Hamilton, runs through theater, jazz and pop.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Okay. So I’m happy. Okay a couple of things to wrap up with. You know usually when I get ready for an interview or most interviewers they do their homework and they might pick four or five topics that they definitely want to get to in the time they have. But those are not always the topics that the interviewees might pick. So I’m wondering if there’s something that you would like to talk about that I haven’t asked or that no one else has ever asked?

Well not that no one else has ever asked, but something I think about all the time is the discontinuity of musical language that happened roughly in the late 60s. And it happened not only in jazz it happened in popular music, it happened in theater music. You know the difference between Gershwin and Arlen, Frank Loesser, Cole Porter, and Andrew Lloyd Weber, there’s a chasm, an absolute chasm. All the rest is continuous music from pre- Bach, through Baroque classical romantic twentieth century music and the threads go back through that and all of a sudden all these threads are broken. That doesn’t make any sense to me. I don’t relate to that. I don’t relate to “Hamilton” as music. It’s discontinuous.
Could it have anything to do with technology?
Everything keeps getting better and better — technology in the theater, lights and sets and all that. And maybe somehow the music was conceived as we don’t need it to be as deep as it used to be.

I don’t know. That’s a good thought. That’s certainly possible. Certainly that is a fact that things have skewed that way. Whether it’s a result or an intention I’m not in a position to judge that. I’m more inclined to think that it’s a result of the same problem that I think pop music has and that is that we reverted to cheap popular music sometime in, kind of in the middle of my lifetime, you know in my 30s and 40s. The things that had built — on which our popular music was built, going back to Stephen Foster and the music my grandmother sang to me, what I heard on the radio when I was a child. You know you heard Cole Porter, you heard Gershwin, you heard Fats Waller, you heard Duke Ellington, you heard all sorts of cheap stuff, but not entirely. And then at a certain point all of that went away, that you no longer heard Rosemary Clooney sing or Bing Crosby sing or Frank Sinatra sing. That that was gone. And for a while there was this Motown music that wasn’t so bad, it had a lot of good things in it. And then pretty much that dissipated too and you have nothing but, well what to me is empty-headed, empty- soulless stuff that doesn’t relate to my experience as a human being. and I don’t feel close to them. I don’t feel that they are — I understand their anger and their displeasure, I mean but I don’t feel connected.
